guerrilla

/guh-RILL-uh/ — rhymes with gorilla (but different meaning) · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A guerrilla is a fighter who belongs to a small, independent band that attacks a larger, official army through ambushes and surprise raids instead of open battles.

The guerrillas ambushed supply trucks and vanished back into the jungle.

Example

A small band of guerrillas in mountainous terrain cannot face the national army in open combat, so they hide in caves and strike army outposts at night, slipping back into the mountains before reinforcements arrive.

Guerrilla captures both the unconventional tactic and the small-band structure—surprise attacks instead of formal battle, independence from official armies. 'Soldier' would miss what makes them different: their methods and scale.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fighter: Fighter is the broadest word here — anyone who fights, from a boxer to a uniformed soldier, counts as a fighter. A guerrilla is one particular kind: a member of a small, independent band that avoids open battle and strikes a larger army through ambushes and raids.

insurgent: An insurgent is anyone who rebels against a ruling government, whatever methods they use — insurgents can field whole armies and fight open battles. Guerrilla names the method and the scale instead: a small band relying on surprise attacks rather than meeting the enemy head-on.

partisan: A partisan is an irregular fighter resisting an army that occupies their homeland — the word tells you the fighter's cause. Guerrilla tells you the tactics: whatever the cause, a guerrilla fights in a small band that strikes suddenly and slips away instead of holding a battle line.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

soldier: a fighter in an official, uniformed army

Where it sits · their role and rank in the conflict

informant → rebel → guerrilla → commander

informant vs. guerrilla: An informant is the least involved figure on this scale, far from a guerrilla: an informant only passes along secrets, while a guerrilla actually takes up arms and fights.

rebel vs. guerrilla: Rebel is broader and milder than guerrilla — anyone who resists authority can be called a rebel, but a guerrilla is a rebel organized into an armed band that stages ambushes and raids.

commander vs. guerrilla: A commander stands above a guerrilla on this scale of rank and power: a guerrilla fights within a small band, while a commander directs whole forces of fighters and plans their campaigns.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — guerr(a): war (Spanish, from a Germanic root (werra, 'strife, war'))

Suffix — -illa: little (diminutive) (Spanish)

Put it together: Spanish guerra ('war') plus the diminutive suffix -illa makes 'little war' — guerrilla warfare is a small, scrappy war of ambushes and raids, and a guerrilla is a fighter who wages one.

Use the root in a new word: war: English war and Spanish guerra both grew from the same old Germanic root meaning 'strife' — which is why a guerrilla is literally a fighter in a 'little war.'

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / military

Guerrilla is a military and historical term—reach for it when describing irregular fighters or unconventional warfare tactics. For a general fighter, use 'soldier' or 'fighter'; for a protester, use 'activist' or 'protester'.
